note: A man gave agents a bill of divorce for his wife and told them: if I do not come back within thirty days, let it be a divorce. He arrived at the end of the thirty days, but the ferry was on the far side of the river and he could not cross. He called out to the people on the other side: see that I have come, see that I have come. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as coming back.
why: The Gemara is testing Rava's view that a condition counts as unmet even when circumstances beyond the man's control caused it. It cites Shmuel's ruling as proof, then answers that a ferry delay is common enough that he should have stipulated for it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who rules that the man's shouting from across the river does not count as his return.

terms.meaning: The written document (in Hebrew, a get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it is written conditionally, to take effect only if he fails to return in time.
The boat used to cross the river. Because it was moored on the opposite bank, the man was stuck on the wrong side when his deadline ran out.

note: A man handed agents a bill of divorce for his wife, saying: if I do not return within thirty days, let it be a divorce. He reached the river at the end of the thirty days, but the ferry was on the other side and he could not cross in time. He shouted to the people across the river: see that I have come, see that I have come. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as a return.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a condition counts as unmet when the failure was beyond the man's control, such as illness. It cites Shmuel's ruling as evidence, then answers that a ferry being on the far bank is a common problem he should have stipulated for.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who rules that calling out from across the river is not a return, so the divorce stands.

terms.meaning: The written document (in Hebrew, a get) a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. This one was set to take effect only if he did not come back in time.

note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry into the family of Rav Haviva and began reciting the wedding blessing from the time of the betrothal, saying he was certain the family would not back out. The match fell through and they did back out. In a second short report, Rav Tahlifa from the Land of Israel came to Babylonia and recited six long wedding blessings; the Gemara says the law does not follow him.
why: The Gemara is asking from when the wedding-celebration blessing may be recited before the wedding. Rav Pappa began at betrothal because the wedding was already prepared; Ravina's case shows the risk of doing so.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A father who began the wedding blessing at his son's betrothal, sure the match would hold.

people.name: Rav Haviva
people.about: Head of the family Ravina's son was to marry into; that family later retracted.

people.name: Rav Tahlifa
people.about: A Sage from the West, meaning the Land of Israel, who came to Babylonia and recited six long blessings.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which legally binds the couple before the wedding itself; in this period it could still be called off by divorce.
The Babylonian Talmud's name for the Land of Israel, which lay west of Babylonia.

flag: Two unrelated short reports (Ravina's son's match, and Rav Tahlifa's six blessings) are joined in one story.

note: The young child of Rav Hiyya bar Abba, teacher of Reish Lakish's sons, died. Reish Lakish did not come on the first day; the next day he came with his spokesman, Yehuda bar Nahmani, and told him to say something about the child. Yehuda quoted verses saying God is angry at a sinful generation and its children die young, which the Gemara explains as telling Rav Hiyya he was important enough to be taken for the generation's sins. Reish Lakish then had him speak in praise of God, for the mourners, for those who comfort them, and for all Israel, and Yehuda closed each with a blessing.
why: The Gemara is asking how a mourners' blessing could be recited throughout the seven days of mourning; it answers that this happens when new visitors arrive, and cites this visit on the second day, with its series of blessings.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Teacher of Reish Lakish's son or sons; it is his child who died.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Comes to comfort his sons' teacher on the second day and directs his spokesman what to say.

people.name: Yehuda bar Nahmani
people.about: Reish Lakish's spokesman, who delivers the words of comfort and the blessings.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Comments that one should say 'many have drunk' but not 'many will drink', so as not to invite disaster.

people.name: Rav Hanan bar Rav
people.about: Explains a verse quoted in the comfort as a warning against speaking obscenely.

terms.meaning: A Sage's spokesman, who repeated and expanded the master's words aloud to a gathering.
A saying meaning one should not speak of possible future disasters, as if inviting them to happen.

note: A man came before Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said that he had slept with his bride and found no blood. She said she had been a virgin. Rabban Gamliel asked for the cloth from that night, had it soaked and washed, and found several drops of blood on it. He told the groom: go, take possession of your acquisition.
why: The Gemara is collecting cases where a groom claims his bride was not a virgin. Right after, Rav Ashi explains why Babylonian judges could not copy this washing test.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he examines the cloth and rules for the bride.

terms.meaning: The judge's way of saying the marriage stands as it was: the bride was a virgin and the groom has no claim against her.

note: A man came before Rabban Gamliel son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said he had slept with his bride and found no blood; she said she was still a virgin. Rabban Gamliel had two maidservants brought, one a virgin and one not, and seated each on the mouth of a wine barrel: the scent of the wine came from the mouth of the non-virgin but not from the virgin. He then seated the bride there, and no scent came from her. He told the groom: go, take possession of your acquisition.
why: It is one of a run of cases about a groom's claim that his bride was not a virgin. The Gemara then asks why he tested the maidservants first, and answers he had only heard of the method and would not shame a Jewish woman for nothing.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel bar Rabbi
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he tests the method on two maidservants before using it on the bride.

terms.meaning: The judge's way of saying the marriage stands: the bride is a virgin and the groom has no claim against her.

note: A man came before Rabban Gamliel the Elder and said that he had slept with his bride and found no blood. She said she came from the Dorketi family, whose women have neither menstrual blood nor the blood of virginity. Rabban Gamliel checked among her female relatives and found that she was telling the truth. He told the groom to take possession of his acquisition and called him fortunate to have married into the Dorketi family.
why: It continues a series of cases of grooms claiming their brides were not virgins. Afterward Rabbi Hanina says Rabban Gamliel's comfort was empty, since a woman without blood will have few children, and the Sages dispute what he actually said.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The judge who investigates the bride's family and confirms her claim.

terms.meaning: The name of the bride's family. The Gemara explains it as 'truncated generation'.
In Jewish law a woman who menstruates is forbidden to her husband for a time; a woman who never does avoids that issue.

note: In years of drought, a man came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and said he had slept with his bride and found no blood; she said she was still a virgin. Rabbi saw that their faces were black from hunger. He had them taken to the bathhouse, fed and given drink, and then brought to a room; the groom slept with her again and found blood. Rabbi told him to take possession of his acquisition, and read over them the verse: their skin is shriveled upon their bones, it has become like a stick.
why: It is the last of a run of cases where a groom says his bride showed no sign of virginity, each showing a different reason the blood may be missing: here, famine. The chapter ends right after it.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; he sees the couple are starving, has them fed, and rules for the bride.

terms.meaning: The judge's way of saying the marriage stands: the bride was a virgin and the groom has no claim against her.

note: Rav Aha used to put the bride on his shoulders and dance. The Sages asked him whether they could do the same. He told them: if a bride is like a wooden beam to you, fine; if not, no.
why: The Gemara is gathering accounts of Sages who danced to bring joy to a bride, such as Rabbi Yehuda bar Elai with a myrtle branch and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzhak juggling three branches.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: A Sage who danced with the bride on his shoulders.

terms.meaning: Rav Aha's test: only someone who feels no more stirred by the bride than by a piece of wood may carry her this way.

note: The Sages taught that a funeral procession turns aside to let a bride's procession pass, and both turn aside for a king of Israel. It was said of King Agrippa that he turned aside for a bride, and the Sages praised him.
why: Right after, the Gemara asks how the Sages could praise Agrippa when a king may not give up the honor due to him, and answers that it happened at a crossroads, where no one could tell he had yielded.

people.name: King Agrippa
people.about: A king who turned his entourage aside to let a bride's procession pass, and was praised for it.

note: A woman of great beauty had many men pressing to marry her, and she told them she was already betrothed. Later she went ahead and betrothed herself to a man. When the Sages asked her why, she explained that the first men were unworthy, so she claimed to be betrothed; now that worthy men had come, she accepted one. Rav Aha Sar HaBira raised this before the Sages at Usha, and they ruled that if she gives a reason for her first statement, she is believed.
why: The Gemara has taught that a woman who said she was married and then said she was not is believed if she gives a reason for her first claim. This incident is cited in support.

people.name: Rav Aha Sar HaBira
people.about: Brought this case before the Sages at Usha for a ruling.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, betrothal is the first, binding stage of marriage. A woman who is betrothed is forbidden to marry anyone else.
The town where the Sages gathered as a high court at the time.

note: Captive women were brought to Neharde'a to be ransomed, and Shmuel's father set guards over them. Shmuel asked who had guarded them until now; his father answered: if they were your daughters, would you treat them with such contempt? Later Shmuel's own daughters were taken captive and brought to the Land of Israel. They left their captors outside, went into Rabbi Hanina's study hall, each said 'I was taken captive, and I am pure', and were permitted. When the captors came in, Rabbi Hanina said these were daughters of great teachers, and it emerged that they were Shmuel's. He told Rav Shemen bar Abba, a priest, to marry one; Rav Shemen objected that there were witnesses overseas, and Rabbi Hanina said those witnesses were not before them.
why: The Gemara has taught that a captive woman who says she stayed pure is believed and may marry a priest, unless witnesses later testify she was violated. Rav Ashi reads Rabbi Hanina's reply about the overseas witnesses in that light.

people.name: Shmuel's father
people.about: Posted guards over the captive women at Neharde'a and rebuked his son's remark.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Questioned his father's guards; his own daughters were later taken captive.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Head of the study hall where Shmuel's daughters made their claim; he permitted them.

people.name: Rav Shemen bar Abba
people.about: A priest and relative of the daughters, told by Rabbi Hanina to marry one of them.

terms.meaning: Here it means she was not violated while in captivity. A captive woman is otherwise suspected of it and may not marry a priest.

terms.term: like an error that comes from the ruler
terms.meaning: A verse from Ecclesiastes, used here to say that the father's words came true, as if decreed: Shmuel's own daughters were later taken captive.

note: Shmuel told of a man who, chatting about something else, recalled being carried as a small child on his father's shoulder: they took him out of school, took off his shirt and immersed him so he could eat teruma that evening. Rabbi Hiyya added that the man said his friends kept away from him and called him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'. On the strength of this, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raised him to the priesthood.
why: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Hiyya could accept a brother's word that a man is a Levite when relatives may not testify. It answers that he meant a remark made in passing, and cites this case to show such remarks are trusted.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who reported this incident, as Rav Yehuda relates in his name.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Gives the end of the story, with the friends' nickname and the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who accepted the man as a priest on the basis of his remark.

people.name: Yohanan
people.about: The man in the story, whose friends nicknamed him 'Yohanan who eats hallot'.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their households may eat, and only in a state of ritual purity.
Plural of halla, the portion of dough given to priests; like teruma, only priests may eat it.
Dipped in a ritual bath to become ritually pure.
Saying something in passing, in conversation about another matter, without any intent to testify. Such a remark is trusted more than a deliberate claim.

note: Rabbi Yosei the priest and Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav reported a case. A Jewish woman had been held as security for a debt in Ashkelon, and her family kept away from her, but her witnesses testified that she had not been alone with anyone or violated. The Sages told the family: if you believe the witnesses that she was held at all, believe them that she was not violated; if not, do not believe she was held.
why: Rav had said that when gentiles rule, even a woman jailed over money is forbidden to her husband. Rava objects with this case from gentile Ashkelon; the Gemara answers it is cited this way only because that is how it happened.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei the priest
people.about: One of the two Sages who testified about this case.

people.name: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav
people.about: The other Sage who testified about it.

terms.meaning: Held by gentiles as security for a debt. This raised the concern that she had been violated, which would forbid her to her husband.
The early code of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses. Rava quotes this case from the mishna's tractate Eduyyot.

note: A man rented his donkey to another and told him not to take the road along the Pekod River, where there was water, but the road through Neresh, where there was none. The renter took the Pekod road, and the donkey died. Before Rava, he admitted taking that road but claimed there was no water on it. Rava accepted his claim, reasoning that if he wanted to lie he could have said he took the Neresh road. Abaye told him this reasoning does not apply when there are witnesses against the claim.
why: Rav Ashi asks whether a woman who says she neither hid nor was violated is believed because she could have told a better lie. The Gemara compares this case, then notes that here water on the road was known for certain.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, who accepts the renter's claim.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objects to Rava that the argument fails where witnesses contradict the claim.

terms.meaning: A legal argument: a claim is believed if the person could have won with an easier lie and did not use it. The Talmud calls this a miggo.

note: A man came to Mari bar Isak, or some say Hana bar Isak, from Bei Hoza'a, saying he was his brother and wanted his share of their father's property. Mari said he did not know him. Before Rav Hisda, the man was told to bring witnesses that he was the brother; he said he had them but they feared Mari, a violent man. Rav Hisda then told Mari to bring witnesses that the man was not his brother, and when Mari objected that the burden of proof is on the claimant, Rav Hisda said this is how he judges him and all violent men like him.
why: The Gemara has said that a maidservant may keep silent but would not also lie, since one does not commit two dishonest acts. It cites this case as proof: the frightened witnesses would hide the truth but would not testify falsely.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: A violent man who refused to recognize a man claiming to be his brother; some name him Hana bar Isak.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The judge, who put the burden of proof on Mari.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: From Genesis; cited by Rav Hisda as one whom his brothers did not recognize, since he left beardless and returned bearded.

terms.term: The burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: The usual rule: whoever wants to take property from another must prove his claim. Rav Hisda reverses it for a violent man.
A district far from the main Jewish towns of Babylonia, so the brother had been away a long time.

note: A betrothed man and woman who had divorced came before Rava over a money matter, while Rav Adda bar Mattana sat before him. Rava placed a go-between to keep them apart. Rav Adda objected that a divorce from betrothal allows direct payment; Rava answered that he could see these two were used to each other. In another version, Rava did not separate them, and it was Rav Adda who urged him to and gave the same reason.
why: A teaching says a priest who owes his divorced wife money must repay her through someone else, so they do not mix. Rav Nahman exempts a divorce from betrothal, since they are not used to each other; this case shows the exception failing.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge before whom the couple came.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: A Sage sitting before Rava, who debates with him about separating the couple.

terms.meaning: In the first, binding stage of marriage, before the wedding. This couple divorced at that stage.
One of the minor tractates of the Talmud, mainly about the laws of mourning, cited here for its teaching on a divorce from betrothal.

note: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said that he testified only once in his life, and on his testimony a slave was raised to the priesthood. The Gemara refuses to believe God would let a righteous man cause such a wrong, and emends: they sought to raise the slave on his word, but did not. He had seen teruma given to a slave in Rabbi Yosei's town, and testified about it in Rabbi Yehuda's town.
why: The Gemara has explained that Rabbi Yehuda's and Rabbi Yosei's towns differed on whether eating teruma proves a man is a priest; this account shows that difference nearly making a slave a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Tells of the one time he testified, which nearly made a slave a priest.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to priests, which only priests and their households, including their slaves, may eat.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the main early code of Jewish law.
Officially recognized as a priest, with the rights of lineage and marriage that come with it.

note: Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Yonatan were standing together when a man came up, bowed and kissed Rabbi Yonatan's foot. Rabbi Hanina asked what this was about. Rabbi Yonatan explained that the man had written his property over to his sons, and Rabbi Yonatan had forced them to feed him.
why: The Sages at Usha ruled that a man who gave his property to his son is still supported from it, and the Gemara asks if the law follows Rabbi Ile'a on this. The forcing implies the sons owed nothing by law, so it does not.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Was standing with Rabbi Yonatan and asked why the man kissed his foot.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: Had forced a man's sons to feed their father; the man thanked him by kissing his foot.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; here, the binding ruling on whether such sons must support their father.

note: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had a stepmother who was using up their father's money on her food. Rabbi Yohanan told them to have their father set aside land for her support. After the father died they went to Reish Lakish, who said that this only added to her support, and threatened that if they did not give her what she needed he would drive Rabbi Yohanan's ruling out of their ears. When they complained to Rabbi Yohanan, he said: what can I do? A man equal to me disagrees with me.
why: Right after, Rabbi Abbahu reports Rabbi Yohanan's own explanation: everything turns on the wording; land given 'for' her support adds to it, while land given 'as' her support fixes it.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Advised his relatives to have their father set aside land for his wife's support.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Ruled that the land only added to the widow's support, and pressed the sons hard to pay.

terms.meaning: The food and support a husband's estate owes his widow under her marriage contract.

note: A divorced woman who did not want to go on nursing her baby came before Shmuel. He sent Rav Dimi bar Yosef to test whether the baby knew her. Rav Dimi seated her in a row of women and carried the baby past them. When the baby reached her he looked at her face with joy, and she turned her eyes away. Rav Dimi told her: Lift up your eyes, get up and take your son. The Gemara then asks how a blind baby could know his mother, and Rav Ashi answers: by smell and by the taste of her milk.
why: The Gemara has ruled that a divorced mother can be made to keep nursing a baby who already recognizes her, and is asking at what age that happens. Shmuel held there is no fixed age, so each baby must be checked; this case shows such a check.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage the divorced woman comes to; he sends someone to test the baby.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: Sent by Shmuel to check whether the baby recognizes its mother.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Explains how a blind baby would recognize his mother.

note: Abaye's tenant farmer asked him whether he could betroth a nursing woman fifteen months after her baby's birth. Abaye said yes, piling up reasons: the law follows Rabbi Yehuda over Rabbi Meir, and Beit Hillel over Beit Shammai; Ulla ruled with Rabbi Yehuda; and Mar Ukva said Rabbi Hanina had let him marry after fifteen months, so a mere betrothal was surely allowed. When Abaye told his teacher Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef answered that Rav and Shmuel both say she must wait twenty-four months. Abaye ran three parasangs after the farmer, and some say one parasang through sand, but he could not catch up with him.
why: The Gemara is discussing how long a nursing widow must wait before remarrying: twenty-four months or eighteen, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel shortening each by three. Afterward Abaye draws the lesson that a student should not rule on even a simple matter near his teacher.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Gives his tenant farmer a lenient ruling, then learns from his teacher that it was wrong.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who cites Rav and Shmuel requiring a twenty-four-month wait.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Rules that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Says Rabbi Hanina allowed him to marry a nursing woman after fifteen months.

terms.meaning: The first stage of Jewish marriage, which makes the couple legally bound to each other; the wedding and living together come later.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly three to four miles.
The two great early schools of Sages; when they disagree, the law generally follows Beit Hillel.

note: Two pious men, who some say were Rav Mari and Rav Pinehas, the sons of Rav Hisda, both fed the waiter who served at their meals. One gave him food before the meal; the other gave it to him after the guests had eaten. Elijah used to speak with the one who fed the waiter first, and did not speak with the other.
why: The Gemara has ruled that a waiter should be given a share of foods with a strong aroma or taste, so he does not suffer watching others eat. Like the story of Avuh and Minyamin bar Ihi just before it, this one shows that even timing counts.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: One of two pious men, by one account sons of Rav Hisda.

people.name: Rav Pinehas
people.about: The other of the two pious men, by one account a son of Rav Hisda.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who speaks only with the brother who feeds the waiter first.

terms.meaning: The biblical prophet, who in Talmudic stories still appears to and speaks with especially worthy people.

note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting at the entrance to the house of King Izgur when the king's chief butler passed by carrying food. Rav Ashi saw Mar Zutra's face go pale with craving, took some food with his finger and put it in his mouth. The butler said he had spoiled the king's meal. Asked why he did it, Rav Ashi said whoever made the dish had spoiled it, because he saw a leprous infection in the meat. They checked and found nothing; he put his finger on one spot, they checked there and found it. When the Sages asked why he had relied on a miracle, he said he had seen a spirit of leprosy hovering over the food.
why: The Gemara has ruled that someone who smells or sees a tempting food should be given some, since the craving can endanger him; this is one of several incidents showing that rule in action.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Feeds Mar Zutra from the king's food and defends himself by finding a defect in it.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Goes pale with craving at the sight of the king's food.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Sits with the other two Sages at the king's gate.

people.name: King Izgur
people.about: The king at whose house the Sages are sitting.

terms.meaning: The biblical skin disease often called leprosy; here the word is used for a defect in the meat that made it unfit for the king.

note: A Roman asked a woman to marry him and she refused. He brought pomegranates, peeled them and ate them in front of her without offering her any. She swallowed the saliva that tormented her until she became ill. At last he asked: If I cure you, will you marry me? She said yes. He brought pomegranates again, peeled and ate them in front of her, and told her to spit out all the saliva that troubled her. She did, until something like a green leaf came out of her, and she was cured.
why: The Gemara has ruled that anyone present when a food with a strong aroma or taste is served should be given some; this story, after the one about Rav Ashi and Mar Zutra, shows how much harm an unsatisfied craving can do.

note: A Jew and a gentile were walking along a road together, and the gentile could not keep up. He reminded the Jew of the destruction of the Temple. The Jew sighed and groaned, but the gentile still could not keep up. The gentile said: Don't you people say that groaning breaks half a person's body? The Jew answered that this holds only for a new sorrow, not for one they are used to, as people say: a woman used to losing her children does not panic.
why: Rav and Rabbi Yohanan have just disagreed over how much of the body groaning breaks, and the Gemara has said the news of the Temple's destruction is especially crushing. The Jew's answer qualifies that: a long-familiar grief no longer breaks the body.

terms.meaning: The central sanctuary of the Jewish people in Jerusalem; its destruction was mourned as the great national catastrophe.

note: Rabbi Abbahu was standing in a bathhouse, held up by two slaves, when the bathhouse collapsed under him. He found a pillar, climbed out and pulled both of them up. Rabbi Yohanan was going up stairs, held up by Rav Ami and Rav Asi, when the stair collapsed under him; he climbed up and pulled them both up. The Sages asked him why, if he was that strong, he needed people to support him. He answered: If so, what will I leave for my old age?
why: The Gemara is defining the 'men of leisure' who, by the mishna, owe their wives marital relations every day. Ravin has just said these are the pampered men of the Land of Israel, and these two incidents are told to show how strong they were.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Climbs out of a collapsing bathhouse and pulls up the two slaves who were supporting him.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Saves himself and his two helpers when a stair gives way, then explains why he still lets them support him.

people.name: Rav Ami
people.about: One of the two who were supporting Rabbi Yohanan on the stairs.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The other of the two supporting Rabbi Yohanan on the stairs.

note: Rav Rehumi studied with Rava in Mehoza and used to come home once a year, on the eve of Yom Kippur. One year he was caught up in his study and did not go. His wife waited for him, saying: Now he is coming, now he is coming. He did not come. She was distressed and a tear fell from her eye. At that moment he was sitting on a roof; the roof collapsed under him and he died.
why: Rav Adda bar Ahava has reported, in Rav's name, that the Rabbis let students leave home for two or three years of Torah study without their wives' permission. Rava says Sages acted on this and it sometimes ended in death; this story is his example.

people.name: Rav Rehumi
people.about: A student of Rava who came home once a year; he dies the year he fails to come.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage in Mehoza with whom Rav Rehumi studied.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, a day of fasting and prayer.

note: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya and son-in-law of Rabbi Yannai, spent his time in the study hall and came home every Friday at dusk. Whenever he came, Rabbi Yannai would see a pillar of fire going before him. One week he was caught up in his study and did not come. When Rabbi Yannai did not see the sign, he told the family: Turn his bed over, for if Yehuda were alive he would not have missed his time with his wife. His words were like 'an error that proceeds from a ruler', and Yehuda died.
why: Shmuel has just said that the proper time for Torah scholars to be with their wives is Friday night; Yehuda keeps exactly that schedule, and the story follows Rav Rehumi's as another death tied to a scholar who failed to come home.

people.name: Yehuda, son of Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: Rabbi Yannai's son-in-law, who studies all week and comes home every Friday at dusk.

people.name: Rabbi Yannai
people.about: Yehuda's father-in-law, who sees a pillar of fire before him and, when it is missing, declares him dead.

terms.meaning: Overturning the beds of the house was a mourning custom; saying it meant treating Yehuda as already dead.

terms.term: an error that proceeds from a ruler
terms.meaning: A phrase from Ecclesiastes 10:5, used here for a great man's mistaken words, which came true anyway.

note: Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) arranged for his son to marry into Rabbi Hiyya's family, but the girl died when they came to write the marriage contract. Looking into the families, they found Rabbi descended from King David's wife Avital and Rabbi Hiyya from David's brother Shimi. Rabbi then matched his son with Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's daughter, with twelve years of study planned before the wedding. When the girl was brought past him, the son cut it to six years; brought past again, he said he would marry first and study after. He was ashamed before his father, who told him he had his Maker's perception. The son then studied twelve years; by his return his wife was infertile. Rabbi said divorce or a second wife would both shame her. Her husband prayed for her, and she was cured.
why: The Gemara is discussing how often Torah scholars owe their wives marital relations, through a run of stories about scholars away at study. This one weighs years of study against a wife's needs, and the price she pays.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Yehuda HaNasi; he arranges two matches for his son and worries over the son's infertile wife.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: His family was the first match for Rabbi's son; the girl died.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
people.about: His daughter became the wife of Rabbi's son; his family agreed to support twelve years of study.

terms.meaning: The document, called a ketubba, written at a Jewish wedding, recording the husband's obligations to his wife.
Rabbi tells his son he acted as God did: according to the two verses, God first planned the Sanctuary for after the people entered the Land, then moved it earlier out of love.

note: At the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding feast, Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai set off for the study hall. Rabbi Shimon asked him to wait so they could go together, but he did not wait. He studied for twelve years, and when he came back the streets of his city had changed and he could not find his house. Sitting by the river, he heard people calling to a girl: Daughter of Hakhinai, fill your pitcher and come. Realizing she was his own daughter, he followed her home. His wife, sifting flour, looked up and saw him; her heart fluttered and she died. He said: Master of the universe, is this the reward of this poor woman? He prayed for her, and she lived.
why: This is one of a string of stories about scholars who leave their wives for years of study, told while the Gemara discusses how often scholars owe their wives marital relations.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
people.about: Leaves for twelve years of study and comes home a stranger to his own town.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: Newly married; asks Rabbi Hananya to wait so they can go to the study hall together.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students gathered to learn Torah, often far from home.

note: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa spent twelve years in the study hall. When he came back he decided not to walk in on his family suddenly, so he sat in the local study hall and sent word home. His son Rabbi Oshaya, whom he did not recognize, came and sat before him and asked him questions of law. Seeing how sharp the young man was, Rabbi Hama was distressed and said: Had I been here, I would have had a child like this. He went home, the son came in too, and Rabbi Hama stood up for him, thinking he had come with another question. His wife said: Is there a father who stands up before his son? Rami bar Hama applied to Rabbi Oshaya the verse 'A threefold cord is not quickly broken.'
why: Rabbi Hama explicitly avoids what ben Hakhinai did in the story just before, whose sudden return stopped his wife's heart. It belongs to the Gemara's run of stories about scholars away from home for years.

people.name: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa
people.about: Returns from twelve years of study and does not recognize his own son.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: Rabbi Hama's son, already a sharp scholar when his father returns.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: Applies the verse about a threefold cord to Rabbi Oshaya.

terms.term: A threefold cord is not quickly broken
terms.meaning: A verse from Ecclesiastes 4:12, applied to Rabbi Oshaya as the third generation of scholars in his family.

note: Rabbi Akiva was a shepherd for the rich ben Kalba Savua. His daughter saw his modesty and asked: If I betroth myself to you, will you go to study? He said yes. Her father heard, threw her out and vowed she would get nothing of his property. Akiva studied twelve years and came back with twelve thousand students. He overheard an old man ask her how long she would live as a living man's widow; she said that if he listened to her, he would study twelve more. Taking that as permission, he left again and returned with twenty-four thousand. She went out in her poor clothes, fell at his feet and kissed them. When his attendants pushed her away he said: Leave her; mine and yours is hers. Her father came to have his vow undone, learned who Akiva was, kissed his feet and gave him half his money.
why: It closes the Gemara's run of stories about scholars who spend twelve years away studying. In the others the wife pays for the absence; here she sends him and asks for more.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A shepherd who becomes a great scholar after twenty-four years of study, sent by his wife.

people.name: ben Kalba Savua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's wealthy employer, who throws out his daughter for marrying Akiva and later seeks him out.

people.name: ben Azzai
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's daughter did for him what her mother had done for Akiva.

terms.meaning: A binding oath; here the father swore his daughter could have no benefit from his property. A Sage can sometimes undo a vow made on a mistaken assumption.
A woman who lives alone for years while her husband is still alive but away.
To enter the first, legally binding stage of Jewish marriage.

note: Rava sent his son, Rav Yosef, to study with the Sage Rav Yosef, and they set the term at six years. After three years, on the eve of Yom Kippur, the son said he would go and see his family. His father heard, took up a weapon and went out to meet him. He said: Did you remember your mistress? Some say he said: Did you remember your dove? The two were so caught up that neither of them ate the last meal before the fast.
why: It ends the Gemara's string of stories about students who leave home for years to study, part of its discussion of what a scholar owes his wife. Here it is the father who will not let the son break off his studies.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: Sent to study for six years; wants to visit home after three.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Yosef's father, who goes out armed to stop his son coming home.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage the son was sent to study with.

terms.meaning: The last meal eaten on the eve of Yom Kippur before the fast begins.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year, observed with a full day's fast.

note: Rav Zevid's daughter-in-law rebelled against her husband and was holding on to a garment. Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi sat with Rav Gamda and said that a wife who rebels loses her worn clothes. Rav Gamda said: Because Rav Zevid is a great man you flatter him? Didn't Rav Kahana say that Rava raised this question and did not resolve it? In another version, the three said she does not lose her worn clothes, and Rav Gamda said: Because Rav Zevid is a great man, you twist the judgment against him? Rava left it unresolved.
why: The Gemara is setting out the law of a 'rebellious' wife. Since the question was never settled, it concludes from this episode that what she has already seized is not taken from her, and what she has not seized is not given to her.

people.name: Rav Zevid
people.about: His daughter-in-law is the rebellious wife; the Sages are accused of bending the law because of his greatness.

people.name: Rav Gamda
people.about: Rebukes the three Sages for ruling on a question Rava left open.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: One of the three Sages who rule on the case.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: One of the three Sages who rule on the case.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: One of the three Sages who rule on the case.

terms.meaning: In this discussion, a wife who refuses her husband marital relations (or, in one view, her household duties); the court reduces what her marriage contract will pay her.
Clothing a bride brought into the marriage as part of her dowry, which may since have become worn but still exists.

note: After Abaye died, his widow Homa came before Rava, the judge, and asked him to set her support. He did. She asked for wine as well. Rava said he knew Nahmani (Abaye) did not drink wine. She swore by his life that Abaye gave her wine in cups this big, and as she showed him, her arm was uncovered and a light shone in the courtroom. Rava went home and asked his wife, the daughter of Rav Hisda, for relations. She asked who had been in court today. He said: Homa, Abaye's wife. She went after Homa and beat her with the lock of a chest until she drove her out of all of Mehoza, saying: You have killed three, and now you come to kill another?
why: The Gemara has been asking whether a widow's support includes wine. Rava assumes it depends on whether she drank in her husband's lifetime; the case after it gives wine by local custom in Mehoza.

people.name: Homa
people.about: Abaye's widow; Rava's wife accuses her of having killed three (the translation explains: three husbands).

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who sets Homa's support.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Homa's late husband, also called Nahmani.

people.name: daughter of Rav Hisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who drives Homa out of the city.

terms.meaning: A widow is entitled to food and upkeep from her late husband's estate; the court sets the amount.
A polite oath addressed to the Sage, like saying 'I swear to you'.

note: Riding out of Jerusalem with his students, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman picking barley out of Arabs' animals' dung. Covering herself with her hair, she asked him for support; she was the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon. Asked where her father's money had gone, she quoted a Jerusalem proverb that money lacks salt, or by another reading that kindness is its salt; her father-in-law's wealth, she said, was lost along with it. She reminded him he had signed her marriage contract; he told his students it listed a million gold dinars from her father alone. He wept: when Israel does God's will no nation rules them, and when they do not, they are handed even to a lowly nation's animals. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok swears he saw her gathering barley among horses' hooves in Akko.
why: The Gemara has just told how the Sages granted Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter four hundred gold coins for perfume from her late husband's estate; this tells what later became of her.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Meets the ruined woman on the road and remembers signing her marriage contract.

people.name: the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: Once immensely rich, now gathering barley from animal dung.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: Her father, a man of vast wealth whose charity the Gemara questions.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Swears he saw her gathering barley among horses' hooves in Akko.

terms.meaning: The document, called a ketubba, written at a wedding; it records what the bride brings and what the husband owes her.
A name for God, meaning the One who is everywhere.

terms.term: According to the camel is the burden
terms.meaning: A proverb: the stronger the camel, the heavier its load. The Gemara uses it to say Nakdimon gave less charity than a man of his wealth should have.

note: Hillel the Elder provided a poor man from a good family with a horse to ride and a servant to run in front of him. One time Hillel could not find a servant to run before him, so Hillel himself ran in front of him for three mil.
why: The Sages read the verse 'sufficient for his deficiency in that which is deficient for him' as requiring charity to supply what a poor person lacks, even a horse and a servant for one who was used to them; Hillel's deed is told as an example.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: Provides a once-wealthy poor man with a horse and a servant, and once runs before him himself.

terms.meaning: A measure of distance, roughly a kilometer or a little over half a mile.

note: A man came to Rabbi Nehemya asking for charity. Rabbi Nehemya asked what he usually ate, and he said fatty meat and aged wine. Rabbi Nehemya asked whether he would be willing to share his own meal of lentils. The man ate lentils with him, and he died. Rabbi Nehemya said: Woe to this one who was killed by Nehemya.
why: After cases of charity giving a once-wealthy poor man what he was used to, this one shows the other side. The Gemara asks why Rabbi Nehemya did not say 'woe to Nehemya', and explains he meant the man was to blame for pampering himself so.

people.name: Rabbi Nehemya
people.about: Offers a poor man used to rich food a share of his own lentils.

note: A man came to Rava asking for charity. Rava asked what he usually ate, and he said fattened hen and aged wine. Rava asked whether he was not worried about burdening the community. The man answered: Do I eat from what is theirs? I eat from what the Merciful One gives, citing a verse that God gives each person his food in his own time. Just then Rava's sister, who had not seen him for thirteen years, arrived and brought him a fattened hen and aged wine. Rava said: What is this before me? and told the man: I have answered you; get up and eat.
why: The Gemara is discussing how far charity must go to meet a poor person's accustomed standard. Coming after the man who died eating Rabbi Nehemya's lentils, this story supports giving such a man what he is used to.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Questions a poor man's expensive tastes, then gives way when the same foods arrive at his door.

people.name: Rava's sister
people.about: Arrives after thirteen years away bringing exactly the food the man asked for.

terms.meaning: A name for God.

note: Mar Ukva had a poor neighbor, and every day he secretly tossed four dinars for him through a slot by the hinge of his door. One day the poor man decided to find out who was doing him this kindness. That day Mar Ukva was late from the study hall and his wife came with him. When the poor man came out after them, they ran and hid in a furnace whose fire had been raked over but was still burning. Mar Ukva's legs were being singed, and his wife told him to rest his feet on hers. He became distraught, and she explained: she is at home, and the help she gives reaches the poor directly.
why: The Gemara has been discussing how charity should treat a poor man who refuses help, and now tells stories of how the Sages gave. It explains their flight into the furnace with a teaching: better to throw oneself into a fiery furnace than to shame another person in public.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Gave charity every day to a poor neighbor without letting him know who the giver was.

people.name: Mar Ukva's wife
people.about: Came with him that day; her legs were spared in the furnace, and she explained why.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.
The house of study where the Sages learned Torah together.

note: Mar Ukva used to send four hundred dinars every year, on the eve of Yom Kippur, to a poor man in his neighborhood. One year he sent the money with his son, who came back and said the man did not need it: he had seen the household sprinkling old wine for him, which the translation explains was to scent the room. Mar Ukva said: he is that pampered? He doubled the sum and sent it to him.
why: The Gemara is collecting stories of how the Sages gave charity. In the very next story Rabbi Ḥanina's wife reports signs of wealth and he concludes the man is not needy; here the same kind of report leads Mar Ukva to give more.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Sent a yearly gift of charity to a poor neighbor.

people.name: Mar Ukva's son
people.about: Carried the money one year and reported that the man did not need it.

terms.meaning: The Day of Atonement, the holiest fast day of the Jewish year.
A silver coin.

note: When Mar Ukva was dying, he asked for his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. He said: My provisions are light and the way is far, meaning, as the translation explains, that this was too little to bring him to the World to Come. He got up and gave away half of all his money.
why: The Gemara uses the story to raise a ruling made at Usha that no one should give away more than a fifth of his wealth, and answers that the limit protects a living person from becoming poor and does not apply at death.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: A generous giver of charity, reviewing his record as he was dying.

people.name: Rabbi Ilai
people.about: The Sage who reports the Usha ruling limiting charity to a fifth of one's wealth.

terms.meaning: A town where the Sages met and enacted a set of ordinances.
The life after this one, in which a person is rewarded for his deeds.
Fine gold coins, according to the translation.

note: Rav Anan sent Rav Huna a letter that opened, Huna, our friend, peace! and asked him to give a woman one-tenth of her father's estate. Rav Huna told Rav Sheshet, who was sitting before him, to carry back a reply, and put anyone who failed to say it under a ban: Anan, Anan! From land or from movable property? And who sits at the head in the house of a marzeiḥa? Rav Sheshet delivered it word for word, saying he would never have spoken so to a teacher except for the ban. Rav Anan took the message to Mar Ukva, admitting he did not know what a marzeiḥa was. Mar Ukva heard the whole story and said: a man who does not know what a marzeiḥa is writes to Rav Huna as Huna, our friend?
why: The Gemara is discussing a daughter's right to a tenth of her father's estate for her dowry, and from what it is paid. Rav Huna's barbed question raises exactly that point, which Rava settles after the story: from land, not movable property.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Wrote to Rav Huna as an equal on behalf of a woman claiming her share of an estate.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Took offense at the familiar greeting and sent a sharp reply.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Sat before Rav Huna and was made to deliver his reply.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Rav Anan turned to him for advice and told him he had overstepped.

terms.meaning: The Gemara explains it means a mourner, citing Jeremiah's words about a house of mourning. The point of the question was who sits at the head among mourners.
Excommunication: a formal ban a Sage could place on someone, cutting him off from the community.
Goods and money, as opposed to land.

note: Ilfa hung himself from a ship's mast and declared: if anyone brings me a teaching from the school of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Oshaya and I cannot show it in the Mishna, I will fall and drown. The translation explains that he did this after Rabbi Yoḥanan was made head of the academy in his absence. An old man came and taught: if a dying man says, Give my sons a shekel a week, and they need a sela, they get a sela; if he said, Give them only a shekel, they get only a shekel; and if he said that others should inherit after them, they get only a shekel either way. Ilfa answered that this follows Rabbi Meir, who says it is a mitzva to carry out the words of the dead.
why: Just before, the Gemara reads the mishna as a dispute in which Rabbi Meir holds that a third party must carry out a dead father's instructions about his daughter's money. Ilfa traces the old man's teaching to that same view of Rabbi Meir.

people.name: Ilfa
people.about: A Sage who staked his life on tracing any teaching back to the Mishna.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: His school's teachings were the challenge Ilfa invited.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: Named with Rabbi Ḥiyya as the source of the teachings.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose view, that the words of the dead must be carried out, Ilfa cites.

terms.meaning: The core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.
Coins; according to the translation a sela is worth two shekels.
A religious duty.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.

flag: The last two STORY segments are not part of Ilfa's story: one is Rav Ḥisda's ruling on the shekel case with the Gemara's discussion, the other quotes a mishna about children's sales that opens the next topic.

note: Rabba bar bar Ḥanna recalled walking behind Rav Ukva when he saw an Arab woman sitting, casting her spindle and spinning red thread opposite her face. When she saw them, she broke the spindle off the thread and threw it down, and said to him: Young man, give me the spindle. Rav Ukva said something about her. Later Sages disagreed about what he said: Ravina said he called her an example of a woman who spins in the marketplace; the Rabbis said, of a woman who speaks with every man.
why: The mishna lists conduct that breaks the customs of Jewish women, including spinning in the marketplace and speaking with every man, and Avimi has just explained spinning as working red thread before one's face. This encounter is offered as such a scene.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥanna
people.about: Tells the story; he was walking behind Rav Ukva.

people.name: Rav Ukva
people.about: Made a remark about the woman.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A later Sage who explained what Rav Ukva's remark was.

terms.meaning: A weighted stick that is spun to twist fibers into thread.

note: Rabbi Yoḥanan warned people to beware the flies of those with ra'atan, and other Sages kept their distance from the sick, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi stayed close to them and studied Torah, saying the Torah protects those who learn it. As he was dying, the Angel of Death was told to do his will. He asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the angel's knife on the way; when shown his place, he jumped in. The angel grabbed his cloak, but he swore he would not come back, and God ruled he could stay since he had never had an oath released. He kept the knife until a Divine Voice ordered him to return it. Elijah announced him, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai asked if a rainbow had been seen in his days. He said yes; the Gemara says none had been, but he would not take credit.
why: The Gemara has been describing the disease ra'atan and its cure. This story sets the Sages who avoided its sufferers against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who stayed with them, and the next story names that devotion as the merit that set him apart.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Warned people about the flies of those with ra'atan.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Studied Torah beside the sick and outwitted the Angel of Death.

people.name: Angel of Death
people.about: Sent to take Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and tricked out of his knife.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who announced Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's arrival in paradise.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
people.about: Found sitting on thirteen golden stools in paradise; he questioned the newcomer.

terms.meaning: A severe disease the Gemara describes: watering eyes, running nose, drooling, and flies resting on the sufferer.
A voice from heaven that speaks in the Talmud's stories.
The translation explains that a rainbow signals the world deserves a flood, so none appears in the lifetime of a completely righteous man.

note: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa was a friend of the Angel of Death. When he was dying, the angel was told to do his will. He asked for thirty days to review his learning, since happy is the one who arrives with his learning in hand, and got them. Then he asked to see his place and to hold the angel's knife. The angel asked whether he meant to do what his friend had done. Rabbi Ḥanina said: bring a Torah scroll and see if there is anything in it I have not kept. The angel asked: did you stay close to those with ra'atan and study Torah? Even so, when he died a pillar of fire separated him from everyone. Rabbi Alexandri asked it to withdraw in honor of the Sages, then of his father, with no effect; in his own honor, it withdrew.
why: It follows straight on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's escape and measures Rabbi Ḥanina against him: without that devotion to the sick he cannot repeat the trick, yet still receives a rare honor. Abaye and Rav Adda bar Mattana then argue over what the pillar meant.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa
people.about: A Sage and friend of the Angel of Death who tried to enter paradise alive.

people.name: Angel of Death
people.about: Sent to take him, and wary of being tricked again.

people.name: Rabbi Alexandri
people.about: Persuaded the pillar of fire to withdraw.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Said the pillar set Rabbi Ḥanina apart from those who had not kept the Torah.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: Answered Abaye with a jab that Abaye's roof had no guardrail.

terms.meaning: A severe disease; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had studied Torah beside its sufferers.
By the Gemara's tradition, a pillar of fire separates only one or two people in a generation.
The Torah requires a railing around a flat roof; the Gemara says Abaye had one, but the wind had just blown it down.

note: A woman who wanted to keep her property out of her husband's hands wrote it over to her daughter. She married and was divorced, and the case came before Rav Naḥman, who tore up the deed. Rav Anan complained to Mar Ukva: see how Naḥman the farmer tears up people's documents! Mar Ukva asked for the details, then said: you mean a document of evasion? Shmuel said that if such a document came into his hands he would tear it up. Rava asked Rav Naḥman his reason: a person does not give away his own property to others, but surely a mother gives to her daughter? Rav Naḥman answered: even against her daughter, a woman puts herself first.
why: The Gemara is discussing a woman's power to sell or give away her property beyond her husband's reach. This case asks whether a deed made only to shield property from a husband is real, and the Gemara then challenges it from a baraita that seems to uphold such deeds.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who tore up the woman's deed of gift.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Objected to Rav Naḥman's ruling.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Heard Rav Anan's complaint and backed the ruling; the translation calls him the Exilarch.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Earlier Sage quoted as saying he would tear up any document of evasion.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Asked Rav Naḥman for the reason behind his ruling.

terms.meaning: A deed written only to keep property away from someone, here a husband, not meant as a real gift.

note: A woman inherited four hundred dinars in Bei Ḥozai. Her husband went to collect it, spent six hundred of his own on the journey, and brought back the four hundred; on the way home he needed one dinar and took it from her money. He came before Rabbi Ami, who said: what he spent, he spent, and what he ate, he ate. The Sages objected that this rule applies when a husband eats the produce of his wife's property, but here he took from the principal, and that counts as an expense. Rabbi Ami replied: then he spent and did not eat, so he takes an oath on how much he spent and recovers it.
why: The mishna lets a husband who spent on his wife's property recover the cost with an oath, unless he has eaten from it. This case tests whether using one dinar of her principal counts as eating.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Ruled on the husband's claim and changed his ruling when the Sages objected.

terms.meaning: A place the translation describes as a remote location in Babylonia.
The produce is what property yields, which a husband may enjoy; the principal is the property itself, which stays the wife's.
A sworn statement before the court, used to support a claim when there is no other proof.

note: A woman brought two maidservants with her into her marriage. Her husband married a second wife and gave one of the maidservants to her. The first wife came before Rava and cried out, but Rava took no notice of her. Those who saw it thought Rava held that whatever a husband does with his wife's property stands. The Gemara says that is not so: his reason was that the maidservant was still serving the household.
why: The Gemara asks whether a husband may sell the produce of his wife's land, and two opposite reports of Rava's view are given. Rav Pappa says the permissive report was only inferred from this case, which the Gemara then reads another way.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who ignored the first wife's protest.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Explains that the permissive report of Rava's view was inferred from this case.

people.name: Yehuda Mar bar Mareimar
people.about: Reported in Rava's name that what a husband does with the produce takes effect.

terms.meaning: The Sages' reason for giving a husband the produce of his wife's property: it is meant to benefit their household.

note: Relatives of Rabbi Yoḥanan seized a cow belonging to orphans in an alley, as the translation explains, because the orphans' father had owed them money. They came before Rabbi Yoḥanan, who told them they had seized it rightly. Then they came before Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, who told them to go and give it back. They went back to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said: What can I do? One who is my equal disagrees with me.
why: The Gemara is weighing why Reish Lakish would reverse judges who ruled like Rabbi Tarfon against Rabbi Akiva, while Rabbi Yoḥanan would not. Here the two Sages rule opposite ways on just such a seizure.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Approved his relatives' seizure, then deferred to his colleague.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish
people.about: Also called Reish Lakish; ordered the cow returned to the orphans.

terms.meaning: Here, the heirs of a man who has died, from whose inheritance his creditors try to collect.

note: Members of the prince's household seized a maidservant belonging to orphans in an alley. Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa were sitting as judges, with Rabbi Abba beside them, and Rabbi Abbahu told the seizers they had taken her rightly. Rabbi Abba objected: because they are of the prince's house, will you flatter them? Judges once ruled like Rabbi Tarfon in such a case, and Reish Lakish reversed their decision. The text does not say how the case ended.
why: It is one of a series of cases about seizing orphans' property for their father's debt. Rabbi Abba treats Reish Lakish's reversal, just told, as binding against the ruling that favored the seizers.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: One of the judges; he upheld the seizure.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappi
people.about: Sat as a judge in the case.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: Sat as a judge in the case.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Sat with the judges and accused them of flattering the powerful.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Cited for having reversed a ruling that followed Rabbi Tarfon.

terms.meaning: The household of the leader of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, as the translation puts it.
Here, the heirs of a man who died owing money.

note: Yeimar bar Ḥashu was owed money by a man who died leaving a boat, and he sent his agent to seize it. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua met the agent and told him that, by Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule, one who seizes for a creditor at the expense of others acquires nothing. Then they seized the boat themselves: Rav Pappa rowed it and Rav Huna pulled it by a rope, and each said he had acquired all of it. Rav Pineḥas bar Ami objected that seizing counts only for goods lying in the public domain; they said they took it from the river's current. They came before Rava, who called them white geese who strip people of their cloaks, and cited Rav Naḥman: a seizure counts only if made while the debtor was alive.
why: The Gemara is gathering cases about creditors who seize a dead debtor's property. This one adds the rule against an agent seizing at others' expense, and ends with Rava's ruling that seizing after the debtor's death acquires nothing.

people.name: Yeimar bar Ḥashu
people.about: A creditor who sent his agent to seize a dead debtor's boat.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Told the agent his seizure was void, then seized the boat himself.

people.name: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Seized the boat together with Rav Pappa, each claiming all of it.

people.name: Rav Pineḥas bar Ami
people.about: Questioned whether their seizure was valid.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rebuked both Sages and ruled their seizure void.

terms.meaning: Space belonging to no one, such as a street or a river's current. Rav and Shmuel say seizing goods acquires them only if they lie there.
Rava's insult; the translation explains it refers to their white beards.

note: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu owed money to people in Bei Ḥozai and sent it with Ḥama son of Rabba bar Abbahu. Ḥama paid them and asked for the loan document back. They said the money had paid other debts, not the one in the document. The case came before Rabbi Abbahu, who asked Ḥama whether he had witnesses that he had paid. He had none. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since they could have said they were never paid at all, they are believed when they say the money went to other debts.
why: The Gemara has been collecting cases on debts and claims in court. Right after this one it asks whether the agent, who handed over the money without getting the document back, must repay the man who sent him.

people.name: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Owed money and sent an agent to repay it.

people.name: Ḥama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
people.about: The agent who paid the debt without getting the document.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Judged the case; Avimi's father.

terms.meaning: A rule of evidence: a person is believed in a claim because he could have made a stronger one and did not.
A place in Babylonia.

note: A woman was required to take an oath in Rava's court. Rav Ḥisda's daughter, Rava's wife, told him she knew the woman was suspected of swearing falsely, so Rava turned the oath over to the other side. Another time, Rav Pappa and Rav Adda bar Mattana were sitting before Rava when a document was brought, and Rav Pappa said he knew the debt in it had been paid. Rava asked whether anyone else knew; no one did, and Rava said that even with the Master's word, one witness is nothing. Rav Adda bar Mattana asked: should Rav Pappa not count at least as much as Rav Ḥisda's daughter? Rava answered: I am certain about her; I am not certain about the Master.
why: The surrounding cases concern oaths and debt documents in court. Right after, Rav Pappa takes from Rava's answer that a judge's personal certainty about someone has legal weight, and the Gemara limits it: it may weaken a document, not tear it up.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A judge who relied on his wife's word but not on Rav Pappa's.

people.name: The daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who warned him the woman could not be trusted to swear.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Said he knew a debt document had already been paid.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: Asked why Rav Pappa was trusted less than Rav Ḥisda's daughter.

terms.meaning: Instead of the defendant swearing she owes nothing, the other party swears that she does and collects.
Jewish law normally requires two witnesses to establish a fact in court.

note: A relative of Rav Naḥman sold the rights to her marriage contract for a sum of money. She was later divorced and died, and the buyers came to claim its value from her daughter. Rav Naḥman said: is there no one to advise her to forgive her mother's marriage contract to her father, and then inherit the money from him? The daughter heard, went and forgave it. Afterward Rav Naḥman said: We have made ourselves like advisers to the litigants. The Gemara explains that at first he held one must not turn away from one's own flesh, and in the end held that an important person is different.
why: The Gemara has just cited Shmuel: one who sells a debt document can still forgive the debt, and so can his heir. Rav Naḥman's advice uses exactly that rule to defeat the buyers.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A judge who gave advice to a relative's daughter and then regretted it.

terms.meaning: The document recording what a husband must pay his wife if he divorces her or dies; she could sell her right to collect it.
The translation explains: like lawyers who coach one side rather than independent judges.

note: A case arose in which a creditor had sold a debt document and then forgiven the debt. Rafram pressed Rav Ashi to rule, and Rav Ashi made him pay as one who damages a beam meant for carving statues, which the translation explains as the full value of the debt in the document.
why: Ameimar has just said that a judge who holds people liable for indirect damage makes such a seller pay the document's full value, while one who does not makes him pay only for the paper. Here Rav Ashi takes the first view.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: Pressed Rav Ashi to give a ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ruled that the full value must be paid.

terms.meaning: Wood meant for carving is worth far more than plain wood; whoever damages it pays its full worth.

note: The estate of the house of bar Tzartzur was small at the father's death and later grew in value. The sons of his two wives came before Rav Amram, who told the sons with the larger claim to go and appease the others. They paid no attention. He said: if you do not appease them, I will strike you with a thorn that draws no blood, which the translation explains as excommunication. He sent them to Rav Naḥman, who ruled that just as heirs keep their rights when a large estate shrinks, so they keep them when a small estate grows.
why: The mishna lets each wife's sons collect their own mother's marriage contract only if the estate exceeds both contracts by a dinar. The Gemara asks what happens when it fell short at the father's death but later grew, and brings this case as the answer.

people.name: bar Tzartzur
people.about: The man whose estate his sons were dividing.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Urged the sons to settle and threatened them when they refused.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Ruled on the case.

terms.meaning: The sum a husband pledges to his wife; under the mishna's rule her sons could inherit it.
Rav Amram's threat; the translation says it means excommunication.

note: A man owed a creditor a thousand dinars. He owned two mansions and sold each for five hundred. The creditor seized one from its buyer and then came to seize the other as well. The buyer took a thousand dinars to him and said: if the house you took is worth a thousand to you, keep it; if not, take the thousand dinars and give up your claim. Rami bar Ḥama thought this was like the mishna's case of orphans who offer to value their father's property a dinar higher. Rava replied: there, the other orphans lose by it; here, does the creditor lose? He lent a thousand and gets a thousand.
why: It follows the mishna's rule that orphans cannot raise the value of their father's estate to gain their mother's marriage contract. Rava's answer shows that rule does not stop a buyer's offer that costs the creditor nothing.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: Compared the buyer's offer to the mishna's case of the orphans.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rejected the comparison.

terms.meaning: A creditor may take land the debtor sold after the loan, because the debt was secured on the debtor's land.
The core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

note: A man owed a creditor one hundred dinars. He had two small tracts of land and sold both to one buyer, fifty dinars each. The creditor seized one tract toward the debt, then came back to seize the other. The buyer went to him with one hundred dinars and said: if the first tract is worth a hundred to you, keep it; if not, take the hundred dinars and give up your claim to both. Rav Yosef thought this matched a ruling in the mishna about orphans and the value of their father's property, but Abaye said the cases differ: here the creditor loses nothing, since he lent one hundred and gets back one hundred.
why: The Gemara has just told the same kind of case with two mansions and a thousand dinars. This smaller version repeats the comparison with the mishna, and the Gemara then asks what sum the buyer's claim against the seller is written for.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who first thought this case was the same as the one in the mishna.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who argued the two cases are not alike, since the creditor loses nothing.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; sums of money in the story are counted in dinars.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses line by line. Here it refers to a ruling about orphans who offer to value their father's property higher than it is worth.

note: A man who owed a creditor one hundred dinars died, leaving only a small tract of land worth fifty dinars. The creditor seized it. His orphans paid the creditor fifty dinars and took the land back, and then the creditor seized it again for the rest of the debt. They came before Abaye, who told them that it is a mitzva for orphans to pay their father's debt: their first payment fulfilled that mitzva, and the creditor's second seizure was lawful.
why: This is one of a run of cases about creditors seizing sold or inherited land. Right after it the Gemara limits Abaye's ruling: had the orphans said the fifty dinars were payment for the land itself, the creditor would have had no further claim on it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the orphans came to; he ruled the creditor's second seizure was lawful.

terms.meaning: A religious duty or good deed commanded by Jewish law. Abaye says paying a dead father's debt is one for his children.

note: A man sold his right to collect his mother's marriage settlement in the future, telling the buyer that if his mother came and objected to the sale, he would not repay him. His mother died without objecting, and then he himself came to contest the sale. Rami bar Hama thought he stood in his mother's place and could object as she could. Rava answered him: he may not have guaranteed the sale against his mother's objection, but did he not guarantee it against his own?
why: The Gemara follows this with another ruling of Rami bar Hama about a sale guarantee, where Rava again objects, this time over whether a guarantee covers the buyer's own creditors.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: A Sage who first thought the son could object in his mother's place.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who answered that the son had guaranteed the sale against his own objections.

terms.meaning: The ketuba: a document promising a wife a sum from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her. Here the son sold his future right to collect his mother's.
A seller's promise to repay the buyer if the sale is later undone by someone else's claim.

note: Rami bar Hama's mother wrote a deed in the morning giving her property to Rami bar Hama, and in the evening wrote another giving it to her other son, Mar Ukva bar Hama. Rami went to Rav Sheshet, who awarded him the property; Mar Ukva went to Rav Nahman, who awarded it to him. Rav Sheshet asked Rav Nahman why. Rav Sheshet's reason was that Rami's deed came first; Rav Nahman replied that we do not live in Jerusalem, where the hour is written on documents. Rav Nahman's reason was the discretion of the judges. When Rav Sheshet claimed the same, Rav Nahman answered that he himself was a judge and Rav Sheshet was not, and that Rav Sheshet had not ruled on that basis to begin with.
why: The Gemara has been debating two deeds dated the same day, and a view that leaves such money to someone's discretion. This case shows two Sages split over the same-day deeds and the discretion of the judges.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: The son who received his mother's property by a deed written in the morning.

people.name: Mar Ukva bar Ḥama
people.about: His brother, who received the same property by a deed written that evening.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: The Sage who awarded the property to Rami bar Ḥama because his deed came first.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who awarded it to Mar Ukva, by the discretion of the judges.

terms.meaning: A written document transferring ownership of property; here two deeds give the same property to two sons.
A rule that when the law cannot decide between two claims, a judge may award the property to whoever he thinks the owner meant to have it.

note: Two deeds came before Rav Yosef for the same property: one dated the fifth of Nisan, the other just 'Nisan' with no day. Rav Yosef gave the property to the holder of the fifth-of-Nisan deed. The other man asked: should I lose? Rav Yosef said he was at a disadvantage, since his deed could be from the twenty-ninth. The man asked for a document letting him collect from the seller's later buyers, from Iyyar on. Rav Yosef replied that those buyers could say his deed was from the first of Nisan, so the field was rightly his. The Gemara gives his remedy: the two deed holders should write each other an authorization to collect.
why: The Gemara has just told of two deeds for the same property written on the same day, morning and evening; this is a second case of rival deeds, decided by how exactly each is dated.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage before whom the two deeds came; he ruled for the holder of the dated deed.

terms.meaning: Months of the Hebrew calendar; Iyyar follows Nisan.
A court document that lets a creditor or buyer seize property, here from people who later bought land from the seller.

note: Someone left coral belonging to orphans in the care of a certain man. The man valued the coral for himself at four hundred dinars and took it. Its value then rose to six hundred dinars. He came before Rabbi Ammi, who asked him: who valued it for you?
why: The Gemara has just explained a ruling that a widow who valued property for herself accomplished nothing, because no one valued it for her; this incident is brought as a parallel, with the same question.

people.name: Rabbi Ammi
people.about: The Sage the man came to; he asked who had valued the coral for him.

terms.meaning: Property belonging to children whose father has died, which the court and those trusted with it must protect.

note: A man rented out his millstone to another, to be paid by the renter grinding for him. Later the owner became rich and bought another millstone and a donkey. He said to the renter: until now I had my grinding done by you; now give me money as rent. The renter answered: I will grind for you. The story itself does not say how the dispute ended.
