why: Ravina compares the case to the mishna's rule that two men who must feed a girl cannot both feed her, so one pays money instead; Rav Avira rejects the comparison, since the owner can keep using the grinding.

terms.meaning: A heavy stone used to grind grain into flour.

note: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called his sons and told them to honor their (step)mother, to keep his lamp, table and bed in place, and that Yosef Heifani and Shimon Efrati, who served him in life, would serve him in death. He came home every Shabbat eve after his death, until a maidservant told a neighbor 'Rabbi is sitting,' and he came no more. He told the Sages where to eulogize him, to reopen the yeshiva after thirty days, that Gamliel would be Nasi and Hanina bar Hama head of the yeshiva. A launderer who missed his funeral threw himself from a roof and died, and was promised the World-to-Come. Rabbi Hiyya and Rabbi Hanina argued over who did more for Torah. Rabbi then passed on wisdom to Shimon and the Nasi's office to Gamliel.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The dying leader who gives his sons and the Sages his last instructions.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: His younger son, called a Sage; Rabbi passes the orders of wisdom to him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: His older son, whom he appoints Nasi.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Named by Rabbi to head the yeshiva; he argues with Rabbi Ḥiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: A Sage praised by Rabbi for teaching Torah to children in towns without teachers.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in the Land of Israel, an office Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi held and passed to his son.
A voice from Heaven that announces a decision or message.
The life after death promised to the righteous.
A house of Torah study.

flag: Very long span: interleaves the deathbed narrative with long stretches of Gemara analysis, and contains the launderer and Rabbi Ḥanina episodes that are also coded separately (7B7829, 3DE90C).

note: On the day of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's funeral, a Divine Voice announced that everyone present at it was destined for life in the World-to-Come. A launderer who came to Rabbi every day had not come that day. When he heard this, he went up to a roof, fell to the ground and died. A Divine Voice announced: that launderer too is destined for life in the World-to-Come.
why: It comes in the Gemara's account of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's death, right after its explanation of his instructions on how he was to be eulogized and mourned.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The great Sage, called simply Rabbi, whose funeral this is.

people.name: the launderer
people.about: A man who came before Rabbi every day but missed his funeral.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that announces a decision or message.
The life after death promised to the righteous.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had instructed that Hanina bar Hama sit at the head of the yeshiva. Rabbi Hanina refused, because Rabbi Afes was two and a half years older than him. So Rabbi Afes sat at the head, Rabbi Hanina sat outside, and Levi came and sat with him. When Rabbi Afes died, Rabbi Hanina took the head seat, Levi had no one to sit with, and he came to Babylonia. Rav was told that a great man who limps had come to Neharde'a and taught that a woman may go out on Shabbat wearing a kelila. Rav concluded that Rabbi Afes had died, Rabbi Hanina had taken his place, and Levi had come.
why: The Gemara is explaining Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's dying instructions one by one; this is how his instruction about Hanina bar Hama came true. The Gemara then asks how Rav knew it was Rabbi Afes, not Rabbi Hanina, who had died.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Ḥanina bar Ḥama, named by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to head the yeshiva; he deferred to the older Rabbi Afes.

people.name: Rabbi Afes
people.about: An older Sage who sat at the head of the yeshiva until he died.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who limps; he studied with Rabbi Ḥanina, then came to Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia who worked out from the news what had happened.

terms.meaning: A house of Torah study; sitting at its head means leading it.
A tiara-like ornament; Levi taught that a woman may wear it in the public domain on Shabbat.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lay ill in Tzippori. On the day he died the Sages fasted and prayed for him, and said anyone who announced his death would be stabbed with a sword. His maidservant first prayed that the lower world would win; seeing his suffering, she prayed the upper world would win. When the Sages would not stop praying, she threw a jug from the roof; in the moment of silence, Rabbi died. Bar Kappara, sent to check, found him dead, tore his clothes and hid the tear, and told the Sages that the angels had seized the holy ark. 'He died?' they asked. 'You said it, I did not.' Dying, Rabbi raised ten fingers and said he had toiled in Torah and taken no benefit. A Divine Voice answered: 'He enters in peace.'
why: This closes the Gemara's long account of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's death. The verse the Divine Voice quotes then leads into teachings about how angels go out to greet the righteous and the wicked when they die.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The great Sage, called Rabbi, whose death this is.

people.name: the maidservant of Rabbi
people.about: His servant, who prays for his release and silences the Sages' prayers.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage sent to check on Rabbi, who breaks the news without saying it.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding verses, worn during prayer and study; Rabbi removed them each time he went to the bathroom.
A voice from Heaven that announces a decision or message.
A sign of mourning made on hearing of a death.

note: Rav Hiyya Arikha's mother-in-law was also his brother's widow. For twenty-five years he supported her in her father's house from his brother's estate. Then she asked for support, and he refused; she asked for her marriage payment, and he said she had lost that too. Rabba bar Sheila ruled that she had not asked out of embarrassment, and ordered him to pay. When he refused, Rabba bar Sheila authorized her to seize his property. Rav Hiyya went to Rava, who said the ruling was good. She then asked Rava for the produce of the land since then. Rava found the authorization did not say the land came from the dead husband's estate, ruled it badly written, and denied her any produce, rejecting her plea to treat the omission as a scribal error.
why: The Gemara has been discussing when a widow loses the right to her marriage payment by long delay. This case applies that to a widow supported for twenty-five years in her father's house, and ends with how an authorization to seize property must be written.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya Arikha
people.about: A Sage who supported his brother's widow, also his mother-in-law, for twenty-five years.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: The judge who ordered him to pay her marriage payment and wrote the authorization.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who upheld the ruling but found the authorization badly written.

terms.meaning: The ketuba: a document promising a wife a sum from her husband's property if he dies or divorces her.
A court document letting a creditor seize a debtor's property in payment.
A mistake by the writer of a document, which a court may treat as if the missing words were written.

note: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei had a sharecropper who brought him a basket of fruit every Shabbat eve. One week he brought it on Thursday, explaining that he had a case to bring before him and was coming anyway. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and said he was disqualified from judging the case. He seated two other scholars to judge it, but as he came and went he kept thinking of arguments the sharecropper could make. He said: blast the souls of those who take bribes. If I, who took nothing, and would only have taken what was mine, feel this way, how much more those who take bribes.
why: The Gemara has taught that even a small favor counts as a bribe, with judges who stepped aside after someone helped them. This case shows that even a gift that is refused leaves the judge biased.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage and judge who refused his sharecropper's early gift of fruit.

people.name: the sharecropper
people.about: A man who farmed Rabbi Yishmael's land and brought him fruit each week.

terms.meaning: A farmer who works someone else's land and pays the owner with part of the crop.
Friday, the day before the Sabbath.

note: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing of his sheep. Rabbi Yishmael asked where he was from, and why he had not given it to a priest closer to home. The man said he had a case to bring before him and had brought the gift on the way. Rabbi Yishmael said he was disqualified from judging the case and would not accept the gift. He seated two other scholars to judge it, but as he came and went he kept thinking of arguments the man could make. He said: blast the souls of those who take bribes. If I, who took nothing, and would only have taken what I was owed as a priest, feel this way, how much more those who take bribes.
why: It follows an almost identical case about Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei and his sharecropper's fruit, in a series of judges who stepped aside after receiving even a small gift or favor.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
people.about: A priest and judge who refused a gift from a man with a case before him.

terms.meaning: The first wool shorn from a flock each year, which the Torah says to give to a priest.
A kohen, a descendant of Aaron, entitled to certain gifts from other Jews.

note: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish and said he had a case to bring. Rav Anan refused and said he was disqualified. The man said he did not need his judgment; he only wanted to give a gift, since a gift to a Torah scholar is like bringing first fruits. Rav Anan accepted it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note saying he could not judge this man. Rav Nahman concluded the man was Rav Anan's relative, set aside a case of orphans to hear his, and the other side, seeing the honor shown, could not argue and lost. Elijah the prophet, who had been teaching Rav Anan, stopped coming. Rav Anan fasted and prayed and Elijah came back, but frightened him, so Rav Anan made a box and sat in it while Elijah taught him the rest.
why: It ends the Gemara's series of judges who refused cases after receiving a gift or favor; here the gift was taken for a good reason, yet it still led another judge to pervert a case.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: A Sage who accepted a man's gift and sent his case to another judge.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who took the man for Rav Anan's relative and heard his case first.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who used to visit Rav Anan to teach him.

terms.meaning: The first ripe produce of the year, which the Torah says to bring to the Temple.
A commandment to do something; Rav Naḥman weighed judging fairly against honoring Torah scholars.
A book of teachings said to come from Elijah, in a longer and a shorter part.

note: In Rav Yosef's years there was a time of divine anger, a famine. The Sages asked him to pray for mercy. He answered: if the prophet Elisha, who supported 2,200 Sages out of his own pocket, did not pray for mercy in a time of anger, should I?
why: Rav Yosef's figure of 2,200 Sages comes from the verse about Elisha's servant setting loaves before a hundred men; the Gemara goes on to derive the number from it and to list how many students stayed on at later academies.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage asked to pray during a famine, who refused.

people.name: Elisha
people.about: The prophet, who Rav Yosef says supported 2,200 Sages and did not pray in a time of anger.

terms.meaning: Asking God to cancel a harsh decree, such as a famine.

note: A man had used a field as a boundary marker in a deed, describing it as someone else's. Later he claimed the field as his own, and then he died, leaving a steward over his orphans' property. The steward came before Abaye, who said the man had lost his claim. The steward said that the father would have claimed he meant only one furrow; Abaye agreed, citing Rabbi Yohanan, and told him to hand over one furrow. That furrow held a row of palm trees, so the steward said the father would have claimed he sold the field and bought it back; Abaye agreed again. Abaye then said: whoever appoints a steward should appoint one like this, who knows how to argue for orphans.
why: The mishna taught that one who names a field as a marker for another loses his claim to it, and Abaye has just limited that rule. This case shows the rule applied, and the claims Rabbi Yohanan allows against it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who judged the case and praised the steward.

people.name: the steward
people.about: The man appointed to look after the dead man's orphans' property.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage whose rulings Abaye cites to accept the steward's claims.

terms.meaning: A neighboring field named in a deed to show where another field's boundary lies; naming it as someone else's admits it is theirs.
A person appointed to manage the property of orphans.

note: Rav Yosef told of a man in Shihin whose father left him three branches of mustard. One broke, and on it alone they found nine kav of mustard, and with its wood they roofed a booth for craftsmen. Rabbi Shimon ben Tahlifa said his father left them a cabbage stalk so tall they went up and down it with a ladder.
why: The Gemara is describing how fruitful the Land of Israel will be in the future, and tells these incidents, like the fox in the giant turnip before them, so the reader will not be surprised.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who tells of the giant mustard plant.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Taḥlifa
people.about: A Sage who tells of a cabbage stalk his father left.

terms.meaning: A measure of dry volume, roughly a liter or two.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, quoted by the Gemara.

note: Rav Hiyya bar Adda taught Reish Lakish's children. Once he stayed away for three days. When he came, Reish Lakish asked why. He said his father had left him one grapevine branch: the first day he picked three hundred clusters, each giving a jugful of wine; the second day three hundred more, two to a jug; the third day three hundred, three to a jug, and he declared more than half ownerless. Reish Lakish told him that had he not stayed away, the vine would have yielded more.
why: The Gemara is collecting stories about the great bounty of the Land of Israel, after expounding verses about its wine.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya bar Adda
people.about: A teacher of children for Reish Lakish, who stayed away three days to harvest a vine.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who employed him and asked why he had been away.

terms.meaning: Gave up ownership so that anyone, especially the poor, may take it.

note: Rami bar Yehezkel came to Benei Berak and saw goats grazing under a fig tree. Honey was oozing from the figs and milk was dripping from the goats, and the two were mixing. He said: this is what the verse means by 'a land flowing with milk and honey.'
why: It is one of a series of reports of the bounty of the Land of Israel; other Sages follow with their own sightings of land flowing with milk and honey.

people.name: Rami bar Yeḥezkel
people.about: A Sage who visited Benei Berak and saw the verse come true.

note: Three Sages each describe what they saw of the land's richness. Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai says that once, rising early on the three-mil road from Lud to Ono, he walked ankle-deep in honey oozing from fig trees. Reish Lakish says he saw the place near Tzippori 'flowing with milk and honey', sixteen mil by sixteen. Rabba bar bar Ḥana says he saw the milk-and-honey land of all Eretz Yisrael, and it was as large as the stretch from Bei Mikhsei to the fortress of Tulbanki: twenty-two parasangs long and six wide.
why: The Gemara is collecting reports of the bounty of the Land of Israel. Just before, Rami bar Yeḥezkel saw goats' milk and fig honey mixing in Benei Berak and called it the meaning of the verse 'a land flowing with milk and honey'; these Sages add their own sightings of that verse come true.

people.name: Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai
people.about: Tells of walking ankle-deep in fig honey between Lud and Ono.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Says he saw the milk-and-honey region by Tzippori.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Says he saw the milk-and-honey land of all Eretz Yisrael and gives its size.

terms.meaning: An ancient measure of distance, roughly a kilometer.
A larger Persian measure of distance, equal to four mil.
Hebrew for the Land of Israel.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and saw grape clusters as big as calves. He asked whether those were calves standing among the vines; the locals told him they were clusters. He cried out: O earth, O earth, gather in your fruit! For whom are you producing it, for these gentiles who stand over us because of our sins? The next year Rabbi Ḥiyya came to the same place and saw clusters the size of goats. When he asked whether those were goats among the vines, the locals told him: Go away, do not do to us what your colleague did.
why: It belongs to a run of stories about the fruit of the Land of Israel. Like the peach that Rabbi Elazar found shrunken a year after his colleagues saw it, the grapes here are smaller the following year, and the locals blame a Sage's words.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sees huge grape clusters in Gavla and tells the earth to stop producing such fruit for gentile rulers.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Visits the same place the next year and is sent away by the locals.

terms.meaning: Non-Jews; here the foreign rulers of the land.

note: On his way up to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Zeira could not find a ferry across the Jordan, so he grabbed hold of a rope and crossed on it. A Sadducee mocked him: You hasty people, who put your mouths before your ears, are still hasty. Rabbi Zeira answered that this was a land Moses and Aaron did not merit to enter; who could say that he would merit it?
why: Just before, Rabbi Elazar rejoiced at each stage of being accepted in the Land of Israel; this begins a run of stories about Sages' eagerness for and love of the Land, followed by Sages who kissed its rocks and rolled in its dust.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who crosses the Jordan on a rope rather than wait to enter the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group that rejected the Sages' teachings; in the Talmud often a hostile questioner.
A jibe at Israel's promise at Sinai, 'We will do and we will hear', which put acting before hearing.
